What one cudaGraphLaunch submits

The API call is a submission boundary, not a kernel. On each TP rank, SGLang asks CUDA to replay one executable graph; CUDA then schedules thousands of graph nodes under the captured dependency constraints.

Representative dependency relationships

Two layers are enough to expose the repeated dependency shapes without drawing 78 nearly identical copies. Layer 6 contains DSA and sparse MoE; layer 3 contains the ordinary MLA and sparse-MoE path. Exact node identities come from the trace. The arrows are reconstructed from captured SGLang source ordering, explicit wait_stream calls, and the observed copy bridge.

74 of 78 layers These two exact shapes recur unchanged: 18 DSA sparse-MoE layers and 56 ordinary sparse-MoE layers.

Evidence boundary

These are source-derived happens-before relationships over exact traced nodes, not an Nsight export of the raw CUDA Graph edge list. A same-queue arrow does not require the earlier kernel to finish before the next kernel begins: dependent launch and graph scheduling can permit physical overlap. The exact raw DAG still requires cudaGraphDebugDotPrint or CUDA Graph dependency enumeration during capture.

Evidence boundary

What this page proves

  • The original captured graph contains 3,281 distinct creation ordinals.
  • Every replay emits 3,202 kernel activities and 75 memcpy activities on rank 0.
  • The same executable shape was replayed 100 times per rank in the 10-by-10 experiment.
  • The atlas binds each kernel ordinal to its audited model operation, layer, source queue, launch geometry, and measured interval.

What this page does not claim

Nsight's SQLite export contains graph-node IDs but no graph dependency-edge table. Adjacent atlas marks are therefore creation ordinals, not asserted parent-child edges.

To render the exact DAG next time, capture the raw cudaGraph_t before instantiation and export it with cudaGraphDebugDotPrint, or enumerate nodes and dependencies through the CUDA Graph API.
